sections.heading: 3.2 Diffusion-based categorical reparameterization
sections.text: id="S3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection"> 3.2 Diffusion-based categorical reparameterization Algorithm 1 Soft reparameterization with DDIM transitions 1: Input: grid ({t_{k}})_{k=0}^{n-1}, schedules (\alpha_{{t_{k}}},\sigma_{{t_{k}}},\eta_{{t_{k}}})_{k=0}^{n-1} 2: Sample x\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\mathbf{I}_{K})^{\otimes L} 3: for k=n-1 down to 1 do 4: \hat{x}_{0}\leftarrow\text{softmax}(\varphi_{\theta}+\alpha_{t_{k+1}}x/\sigma^{2}_{t_{k+1}}) 5: \hat{x}_{1}\leftarrow(x^{i}-\alpha_{t_{k+1}}\hat{x}_{0})/\sigma_{t_{k+1}} 6: \mu\leftarrow\alpha_{{t_{k}}}\hat{x}_{0}+(\sigma_{{t_{k}}}^{2}-\eta_{{t_{k}}}^{2})^{1/2}\hat{x}_{1} 7: x\leftarrow\mu+\eta_{{t_{k}}}z with z\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\mathbf{I}_{K})^{\otimes L} 8: end for 9: return x We now introduce our diffusion-based soft reparameterization of \pi_{\!\theta}. This reparameterization is built upon a DDM with target \pi^{\theta}_{0}=\pi_{\!\theta}. Since \pi_{\!\theta} is a discrete measure, the resulting denoising distribution denoted by \pi^{\theta}_{\!\,0\mathrel{\raisebox{0.45206pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\mid$}}t} is itself discrete. Indeed, following ( 8 ) and the factorization ( 2 ), \pi^{\theta}_{\!\,0\mathrel{\raisebox{0.45206pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\mid$}}t}(x_{0}|x_{t})\propto\prod_{i=1}^{L}\pi^{\theta,i}_{\!\,0\mathrel{\raisebox{0.45206pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\mid$}}t}(x^{i}_{0}|x^{i}_{t}) where \textstyle\pi^{\theta,i}_{\!\,0\mathrel{\raisebox{0.45206pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\mid$}}t}(x^{i}_{0}|x^{i}_{t})\propto\pi^{i}_{\!\theta}(x^{i}_{0})\mathrm{N}(x^{i}_{t};\alpha_{t}x^{i}_{0},\sigma^{2}_{t}\mathbf{I}_{K})\;. With this structure, the posterior-mean denoiser \hat{x}^{\theta}_{0}(x_{t},t)\coloneqq\sum_{x_{0}}x_{0}\,\pi^{\theta}_{\!\,0\mathrel{\raisebox{0.45206pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\mid$}}t}(x_{0}|x_{t}) simplifies to a matrix of posterior probabilities because of the one-hot structure; i.e. we have for any i\in[L] and j\in[K] that \hat{x}^{\theta}_{0}(x_{t},t)^{ij}=\pi^{\theta,i}_{\!\,0\mathrel{\raisebox{0.45206pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\mid$}}t}(e_{j}|x_{t}) and the denoiser can be computed exactly and efficiently. Indeed, since \|x^{i}_{t}-\alpha_{t}e_{j}\|^{2}=\|x^{i}_{t}\|^{2}-2\alpha_{t}x^{ij}_{t}+\alpha^{2}_{t}, we get \displaystyle\hat{x}^{\theta}_{0}(x_{t},t)^{ij} \displaystyle=\frac{\pi^{i}_{\!\theta}(e_{j})\exp(-\frac{\|x^{i}_{t}\|^{2}-2\alpha_{t}x^{ij}_{t}+\alpha^{2}_{t}}{2\sigma^{2}_{t}})}{\sum_{k=1}^{K}\pi^{i}_{\!\theta}(e_{k})\exp(-\frac{\|x^{i}_{t}\|^{2}-2\alpha_{t}x^{ik}_{t}+\alpha^{2}_{t}}{2\sigma^{2}_{t}})} \displaystyle=\frac{\pi^{i}_{\!\theta}(e_{j})\exp(\alpha_{t}x^{ij}_{t}/\sigma^{2}_{t})}{\sum_{k=1}^{K}\pi^{i}_{\!\theta}(e_{k})\exp(\alpha_{t}x^{ik}_{t}/\sigma^{2}_{t}))}\;. This yields the following simple matrix form for the denoiser: \hat{x}^{\theta}_{0}(x_{t},t)=\text{softmax}(\varphi_{\theta}+\alpha_{t}x_{t}/\sigma^{2}_{t})\;.\vskip 2.84544pt (10) Unlike standard diffusion models that learn an approximate denoiser via a neural network, here the denoiser \hat{x}^{\theta}_{0}(\cdot,t) admits a closed-form expression thanks to the factorized categorical structure. This allows reverse transitions from \pi_{1} to \pi_{\!\theta} free of denoiser approximation and results in an approximate and differentiable sampling procedure. For simplicity we consider only the deterministic sampler corresponding to \eta_{s}=0 for all s\in[0,1]. Define T^{\theta}_{s\mathrel{\raisebox{0.45206pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\mid$}}t}(x_{t})\coloneqq(\alpha_{s}-\alpha_{t}\sigma_{s}/\sigma_{t})\hat{x}^{\theta}_{0}(x_{t},t)+{\sigma_{s}}x_{t}/\sigma_{t}\;. (11) Finally, define for all k \smash{T^{\theta}_{t_{k}}(x_{1})\coloneqq T^{\theta}_{t_{k}\mathrel{\raisebox{0.45206pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\mid$}}t_{k+1}}\circ\dotsc\circ T^{\theta}_{t_{n-2}\mathrel{\raisebox{0.45206pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\mid$}}t_{n-1}}(x_{1})}\;. (12) Then, T^{\theta}_{t_{k}}(X_{1}) with X_{1}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\mathbf{I}_{K})^{\otimes L} is an approximate sample from the Gaussian mixture with density \pi^{\theta}_{\!\,{t_{k}}}(x_{t_{k}})\coloneqq\sum_{x_{0}}\prod_{i=1}^{L}\mathrm{N}(x^{i}_{t_{k}};\alpha_{t_{k}}x^{i}_{0},\sigma^{2}_{t_{k}}\mathbf{I}_{K})\pi_{\!\theta}(x_{0}) and in particular, T^{\theta}_{0}(X_{1}) is the approximate and relaxed sample from \pi_{\!\theta} that we use to compute the gradient estimator in ( 7 ). Note that with a single diffusion step, the reparameterized sample is T^{\theta}_{0}(X_{1})=\hat{x}^{\theta}_{0}(X_{1},1)=\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{\!\theta}}[X_{0}], because of the boundary condition \alpha_{1}=0, and we recover the Straight-Through estimator. On the other hand, using many diffusion steps and well-placed timesteps ({t_{k}})_{k=0}^{n-1} yields an almost exact reparameterization of \pi_{\!\theta}. As discussed previously, this is precisely what we want to avoid: the mapping becomes nearly piecewise constant in \theta and we end up with a high-variance reparameterized gradient. This trade-off is directly analogous to the temperature parameter \tau in Gumbel-Softmax relaxations, where a high temperature yields a relaxed but biased approximation whereas a low temperature recovers a high-variance estimator. In our case, the role of the relaxation parameter is played by the number of diffusion steps and the placement of the timesteps ({t_{k}})_{k=1}^{n-1}. More precisely, we show in Proposition 3.1 that the earliest timestep {t_{1}} governs the behaviour of the reparameterized gradient: as {t_{1}}\to 0, the last DDIM step T^{\theta}_{0\mathrel{\raisebox{0.45206pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\mid$}}{t_{1}}} collapses almost all points in {\mathbb{R}}^{K} onto a single one–hot vector, and as consequence, the Jacobian of T^{\theta}_{0} w.r.t. \theta vanishes. We make this intuition precise by considering next, and w.l.o.g, the case L=1 and \varphi_{\theta}=\theta\in{\mathbb{R}}^{K}. We consider the DDIM map T^{\theta}_{0} as a function of the input noise x_{1} and {t_{1}}\in(0,1) while the remaining steps {t_{k}} with k\geq 2 are fixed. For this reason we make the dependence on the timesteps {t_{1:n-1}} explicit and write (x_{1},{t_{1:n-1}})\mapsto T^{\theta}_{0}(x_{1};{t_{1:n-1}}) for T^{\theta}_{0}. The proof is given in Appendix A . Proposition 3.1 (Informal) . Under assumptions stated in the Appendix, and with the timesteps ({t_{k}})_{k=2}^{n-1} fixed, we have for all \theta\in\Theta, \lim_{{t_{1}}\to 0}\big\|\operatorname{J}_{\theta}\!T^{\theta}_{0}(X_{1};{t_{1:n-1}})\big\|=0\;,\quad\mathbb{P}-\text{a.s.} (13) with X_{1}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\mathbf{I}_{K}). The proof relies on the fact that for any t\in(0,1] and x\in{\mathbb{R}}^{K} \displaystyle\begin{cases}\operatorname{J}_{\theta}\!T^{\theta}_{0\mathrel{\raisebox{0.45206pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\mid$}}t}(x)&=\Sigma^{\theta}_{t}(x),\\ \operatorname{J}_{x}\!T^{\theta}_{0\mathrel{\raisebox{0.45206pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\mid$}}t}(x)&=\alpha_{t}\Sigma^{\theta}_{t}(x)\big/\sigma^{2}_{t}\;,\end{cases} (14) with \Sigma^{\theta}_{t}(x)\!\coloneqq\!\mathbb{C}\mathrm{ov}_{\pi^{\theta}_{0|t}(\cdot|x)}(X_{0}). \pi^{\theta}_{0\mathrel{\raisebox{0.45206pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\mid$}}t}(\cdot|x) is a categorical distribution with probability vector \text{softmax}(\theta+\alpha_{t}x/\sigma^{2}_{t}) and under the assumption that \alpha_{t}/\sigma^{2}_{t}\rightarrow\infty as t\rightarrow 0 it collapses into a Dirac delta unless x has at least two coordinates equal to \max_{i}x^{i}. This leads us to consider the decision boundary \mathsf{H}:=\bigcup_{j\neq k}\{x\in\mathbb{R}^{K}:x^{j}=x^{k}=\max_{i}x^{i}\}. Outside of this set, the norm of \Sigma^{\theta}_{t}(x) goes to 0 when t\to 0 as fast as \exp(-\alpha_{t}L(x,\theta)/\sigma^{2}_{t}) where L(x,\theta)>0. Thus, both the Jacobians ( 14 ) go to 0. We then get the result by assuming that the limit, as {t_{1}}\to 0, of the DDIM trajectories T^{\theta}_{{t_{1}}}(X_{1}), with X_{1}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\mathbf{I}_{K}), land outside of \mathsf{H} almost surely. We illustrate Proposition 3.1 in Figure 1 . Figure 1: Visualization of the DDIM transport for \pi_{\!\theta}=\theta\!\cdot\!\updelta_{-2}+(1-\theta)\!\cdot\!\updelta_{2} with the linear schedule (\alpha_{t},\sigma_{t})=(1-t,t). First two rows : DDIM trajectories with varying {t_{1}} for two different values of \theta\in[0,1]. Third row : The DDIM map \theta\mapsto T^{\theta}_{0}(x_{1};t_{1:n-1}) for fixed input quantiles z and three different values of {t_{1}}. \Phi stands for the standard Gaussian cdf. Following the previous discussion, the timestep {t_{1}} must be therefore be chosen in an intermediate regime, small enough to reduce the bias but not so small that the gradients become uninformative.

sections.heading: 3.4 Parameter dependent \pi_{1}.
sections.text: id="S3.SS4" class="ltx_subsection"> 3.4 Parameter dependent \pi_{1}. In the previous construction, the terminal distribution p_{1} is fixed to a standard Gaussian \pi_{1}=\mathcal{N}(0,\mathbf{I}_{K})^{\otimes L}. In our setting, however, we can exploit the factorization ( 2 ) to choose a parameter–dependent Gaussian distribution \pi^{\theta}_{1} that best approximates \pi_{\!\theta} in the maximum–likelihood sense. Formally, we take \pi^{\theta}_{1} with factorized density \pi^{\theta}_{1}(x)=\prod_{i=1}^{L}\mathrm{N}(x^{i};\mu^{i}_{\theta},\mathrm{Diag}(v^{i}_{\theta})) where for all i\in[L], (\mu^{i}_{\theta},v^{i}_{\theta})\in{\mathbb{R}}^{K}\times{\mathbb{R}}^{K}_{>0} and \mathrm{Diag}(v^{i}_{\theta})\in{\mathbb{R}}^{K\times K} is a diagonal matrix with v^{i}_{\theta} as diagonal entries. The parameters are then defined as any solution of the maximum–likelihood problem \{(\mu^{i}_{\theta},v^{i}_{\theta})\}_{i=1}^{L}\;\in\;\argmax_{\{(\mu^{i},v^{i})\}_{i=1}^{L}}\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{\!\theta}}\bigl[\log\pi^{\theta}_{1}(X_{0})\bigr], where, due to the factorization of \pi^{\theta}_{1}, the loss writes equivalently as \sum_{i=1}^{L}\mathbb{E}_{\pi^{i}_{\!\theta}}\bigl[\log\mathrm{N}(X_{0}^{i};\mu^{i}_{\theta},\mathrm{Diag}(v^{i}_{\theta}))\bigr]. For each i, this is exactly the standard MLE problem for a multivariate Gaussian with diagonal covariance, whose one solution is given by matching the mean and per–coordinate variances of \pi^{i}_{\!\theta}; i.e. \mu^{i}_{\theta}=\mathbb{E}_{\pi^{i}_{\!\theta}}[X^{i}_{0}] and v^{i}_{\theta}=\mu^{i}_{\theta}\odot(1-\mu^{i}_{\theta}). We restrict ourselves to a diagonal covariance in order to avoid expensive matrix inversions in the denoiser expression derived next. Data–dependent base distributions of this kind have also been considered in other applications, see for instance Lee et al. (2022) ; Popov et al. (2021) ; Ohayon et al. (2025) . When using the base distribution \pi^{\theta}_{1} and setting \eta_{s}=0 for all s\in[0,1], the DDIM map ( 11 ) keeps the same form as before. The denoiser, however, is different and is now given in matrix form by \hat{x}^{\theta}_{0}(x_{t},t)\!=\!\text{softmax}(\varphi_{\theta}+\frac{\alpha_{t}\lambda_{\theta}}{\sigma^{2}_{t}}\odot(x_{t}-\sigma_{t}\mu_{\theta}-\frac{\alpha_{t}}{2}\mathbf{1})). where \lambda_{\theta}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{L\times K} with \lambda^{i,j}_{\theta}=1/v^{i,j}_{\theta} and \mathbf{1}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{L\times K} is the all-ones matrix. See Section C.2 for a derivation and Appendix C for the DDIM sampler with arbitrary schedule (\eta_{s})_{s\in[0,1]}. We refer to the resulting gradient estimator as ReDGE-Cov .

sections.heading: 4 Experiments
sections.text: id="S4" class="ltx_section"> 4 Experiments In this section, we conduct an empirical evaluation of our method on several benchmark problems, including polynomial programming, Sudoku problem solving, and applications to variational inference and generative modeling. We compare our method against three representative baselines from the literature: the Straight-Through (ST) estimator ( Bengio et al., 2013 ) , the Gumbel-Softmax estimator (more precisely, its Straight-Through variant) ( Jang et al., 2017 ) , and the more recent ReinMax method ( Liu et al., 2023a ) . Among these, ReinMax reports state-of-the-art performance on most of the benchmarks it considers and, to the best of our knowledge, is one of the most recent approaches addressing the same class of problems as ours. For this reason, and since Liu et al. (2023a) show that ReinMax consistently outperforms several earlier alternatives, we do not include additional baselines in our comparison. All the hyperparameters are detailed in Table 5 . For ReDGE and its variants we use the linear schedule (\alpha_{t},\sigma_{t})=(t,1-t) and {t_{k}}=k/(n-1) for k\in[0:n-1] where n is the number of diffusion steps. We use ReDGE-Max with \pi_{1}=\mathcal{N}(0,\mathbf{I}_{K})^{\otimes L} as initialization. Finally, we use the hard gradient estimator for each method.

sections.heading: 4.1 Polynomial programming
sections.text: id="S4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection"> 4.1 Polynomial programming We illustrate our approach on the polynomial programming toy problem also considered in Tucker et al. (2017) ; Grathwohl et al. (2018) ; Paulus et al. (2020a) ; Liu et al. (2023a) . The factorized distribution \pi_{\!\theta} is such that for all i\in[L], \pi^{i}_{\!\theta}=\text{Bernoulli}(\frac{\exp(\theta^{i2})}{\exp(\theta^{i1})+\exp(\theta^{i2})}) with \theta\in{\mathbb{R}}^{L\times 2}. Following prior works, we consider a fixed target vector c=0.45 and solve the optimization problem \textstyle\min_{\theta\in{\mathbb{R}}^{L\times 2}}\frac{1}{L}\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{\!\theta}}\left[\|X\!\cdot\!(0\,\,\,1)^{\top}-c\!\cdot\!\mathbf{1}_{L}\|_{p}^{p}\right], (16) for a fixed exponent p\geq 1 and with L=128. The optimal policy is the one that puts all the mass on the matrix with e_{1} in each row. We report results on this benchmark in Fig. 2 . We also emphasize several limitations of this example, which to our knowledge have not been explicitly discussed in the gradient-estimation literature and somewhat undermine its relevance as a stand-alone evaluation: Figure 2: Polynomial programming benchmark for different values of the exponent p. (1). The objective is separable and identical across dimensions, so the gradient can be recovered from only two loss evaluations (one per coordinate value). (2). ST estimator performs poorly in this experiment. However, note that discrete objective is determined entirely by the values of f at the vertices of the product simplex. Consequently, any extension on {\mathbb{R}}^{L\times 2} that matches f on these vertices defines the same discrete problem, yet may induce a very different optimization landscape. As an illustration, consider the extension \textstyle f:\ x\in\mathbb{R}^{L\times 2}\ \mapsto\ \frac{1}{L}\sum_{i=1}^{L}(-c)^{p}x^{i1}+(1-c)^{p}x^{i2}\;, which is linear and coincides with ( 16 ) on the vertices. For this relaxation, hard ST yields a low-variance unbiased gradient estimator (and soft ST yields the exact gradient) that performs well. See Appendix D.3 for results with this linear relaxation. (3). Finally, ReinMax is based on a second-order Taylor approximation of f. Hence, when p=2 in ( 16 ) the estimator is exact (proof in Appendix B.2 ); for other degrees it is no longer exact, though it often remains a close approximation in practice. This exactness is specific to quadratic objectives and does not extend to general f.

sections.heading: Runtime.
sections.text: id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph"> Runtime. Our method introduces extra computation from the number of diffusion steps used. However, like Straight-Through and Gumbel-Softmax , each gradient estimate requires only a single evaluation of the objective f, unlike REBAR/RELAX and related variance-reduction methods which typically require multiple evaluations ( Tucker et al., 2017 ; Grathwohl et al., 2018 ; Liu et al., 2019 ) . The cost incurred by the number of diffusion steps is an f-independent additive overhead and is negligible in our settings where evaluating f (e.g., a network forward pass or constraint computation) dominates runtime. Hence, our runtime is comparable to the competitors, since we use a small number of diffusion steps (typically 3 to 5). Runtime measurements are provided in Table 4 . Table 4: Average runtime per training epoch for the Categorical VAE experiment with L=48,\,K=2. We report the mean and standard deviation over epochs (in seconds). Sampler Time per epoch (s, mean \pm std) Gumbel-Softmax 5.16\pm 0.07 Straight-Through 5.20\pm 0.20 ReinMax 5.39\pm 0.15 ReDGE 5.80\pm 0.32 ReDGE-Max 6.64\pm 0.21 ReDGE-Cov 6.15\pm 0.24

sections.heading: 5 Conclusion
sections.text: id="S5" class="ltx_section"> 5 Conclusion We introduced ReDGE , a diffusion-based approach to categorical reparameterization that leverages the fact that, for categorical distributions supported on simplex vertices, the denoiser is available in closed form, yielding a training-free differentiable sampling map from Gaussian noise to \pi_{\!\theta}. We analyzed the small-noise regime (playing the role of a temperature) and explained how near-constant transport regions and sharp decision boundaries arise as the relaxation tightens, leading to uninformative gradients. The resulting family of estimators includes practical hard variants and recovers Straight-Through and ReinMax as one-step special cases, while allowing parameter-dependent initializations that improve performance with limited diffusion overhead. A natural direction for future work is to explicitly correct for the residual bias. Our construction already contains all the ingredients needed for REBAR/RELAX-style control variates: a differentiable soft reparameterization, an almost exact parameter-free discrete reparameterization, and even an approximate differentiable conditional reparameterization via a forward–backward DDIM process.
